Who are we, that we should be chained to a regime we did not choose, in a union that no longer reflects our values, governs by our consent, or serves our interests?

Every people on Earth, by the natural rights of man, possess the authority to determine their own form of government. The American Revolution itself was an act of secession—a declaration that a distant, unresponsive, overreaching power no longer represented the will of the governed. We hold this truth to be self-evident, and we have no right to deny to others the right we claimed for ourselves.

Hypocrisy is the only word for a nation that fought its own war of independence while denying that right to its constituent parts.

The Federal Government Was Never Meant to Be This

Let us remember what the founders intended. The federal government was to be one of enumerated powers—narrow, limited, restrained. It was to handle only those things the states could not: defense, the regulation of interstate commerce, the coining of money. Everything else—the education of your children, the regulation of your communities, the moral and civic life of your society—was to remain in the hands of the people themselves, acting through their state and local institutions.

Read the Tenth Amendment: "The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people."

This was not a suggestion. It was the very architecture of liberty. And for generations, that architecture has been dismantled, brick by brick, by judges and bureaucrats and presidents who swore an oath to defend it and then set about destroying it.

The Right of Withdrawal Is the Ultimate Safeguard

Make no mistake: the right of secession is not a call to chaos. It is the final guarantee that government remains just. When all other checks fail—when the ballot is corrupted, when the courts are packed, when the bureaucracy is unaccountable—the right of a people to withdraw from a compact is the last and most sacred defense of liberty.

It is a right that has been recognized in theory by the founders themselves. It is a right that has been exercised in practice by every nation that has ever thrown off the yoke of tyranny. It is a right that exists, whether our courts acknowledge it or not, in the very nature of free men and free women.

You cannot consent to be governed if you cannot withdraw your consent.

A Call to Defend What Is Ours

So I say to you today: be not deceived. The Union that exists today is not the Union of 1789. It is not the Union of the founders. It is a centralized empire that wears the skin of a constitutional republic while feeding on the liberties of its people.

And I say further: every state that still remembers the meaning of sovereignty, every state that still cherishes the liberties that once made this nation a beacon to the world, every state that refuses to be a vassal of a distant, unaccountable, and tyrannical federal apparatus—has the right, and the duty, to assert its independence.

Not as an act of rebellion, but as an act of restoration. Not as a rejection of America, but as a return to the America our founders envisioned—a confederation of free states, bound by ties of commerce and friendship, but each mistress of her own destiny.

Let the tyrants in Washington tremble at this message. Let them know that the spirit of 1776 is not dead. Let them know that the same blood that was shed at Lexington and Concord, at Yorktown and New Orleans, still runs in the veins of free men and women who will not bow to a government that has forgotten its purpose and betrayed its trust.

Closing

The question is not whether secession is convenient. The question is not whether it is popular. The question is whether liberty is worth defending—and I tell you that it is. It has always been worth the cost. It will always be worth the cost.

A government that cannot be resisted is a government that will not be restrained. A people that cannot withdraw from tyranny are a people in chains, however comfortable those chains may be.

Let us therefore resolve—each in our own states, each in our own communities, each in our own hearts—that the right of self-determination shall not perish from this earth while there remains one American willing to defend it.

May God bless these sovereign states. May God bless the cause of liberty. And may God grant us the courage to do what must be done, when the hour demands it.

Thank you.

"The Union is sacred, but liberty is more sacred still."

The United States Constitution, drafted in 1787, established a federal system designed to balance centralized authority with state autonomy. Yet, the question of whether individual states possess the right to unilaterally secede from the Union remains contentious, overshadowed by the legacy of the Civil War. Advocates for secession argue that this right is rooted in foundational constitutional principles, the inherent doctrine of self-determination, and the necessity of resisting federal overreach. By examining these pillars, this essay contends that states retain a moral and constitutional prerogative to secede when faced with systemic tyranny, ensuring the preservation of liberty and democratic governance.

Constitutional Foundation: The Tenth Amendment and the Compact Theory

Central to the argument for unilateral secession is the Tenth Amendment, which stipulates that “powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution… are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” This clause enshrines the principle that the federal government’s authority is strictly limited. Proponents of secession argue that since the Constitution is a compact among the states—rather than a centralized entity dictating terms—the states retain inherent sovereignty. As Thomas Jefferson remarked, the Constitution should be interpreted as binding the federal government, not the states, to its enumerated powers. If the federal government breaches this compact, states have the right to terminate it, much like parties in a contract may dissolve their agreement upon grievous violation.

Furthermore, the Constitution lacks explicit language prohibiting secession. While the post-Civil War Texas v. White (1869) decision declared the Union “indissoluble,” critics argue this ruling was politically motivated, emerging during a period of Reconstruction aimed at consolidating federal dominance. The Founding Fathers, many of whom hailed from states deeply suspicious of centralized power, would likely not have envisioned such an interpretation. The absence of a definitive prohibition in the Constitution itself lends credence to the legitimacy of secession as a constitutional remedy.

Self-Determination Doctrine: Echoes of the Declaration of Independence

The Declaration of Independence, a cornerstone of American political philosophy, asserts that “whenever any Form of Government becomes destructive of [its] ends, it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it.” This principle of self-determination extends to collective entities such as states. If the federal government systematically undermines individual liberties or the consent of the governed, secession becomes a moral imperative. As James Madison wrote in Federalist 49, the people’s “superior force” could compel legislators to safeguard constitutional order. A state, acting on behalf of its citizens, must retain the ultimate tool—the power to withdraw—to defend against federal tyranny.

This doctrine does not advocate chaos but rather reinforces the notion that government is a fiduciary relationship. When the federal government ceases to act in the public’s interest, secession is a peaceful, democratic response to reassert self-governance. The right to secede, therefore, is not about rebellion but a reaffirmation of the foundational ideals of 1776.

Federal Overreach as a Catalyst for Secession

Federal overreach has become a defining characteristic of modern governance, with the executive branch and Congress often exceeding constitutional mandates. From expansive environmental regulations to mandatory healthcare provisions, the federal government’s reach increasingly infringes on areas traditionally reserved to the states. When federal mandates force states to implement policies contrary to their citizens’ will—such as the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) prior to Obergefell v. While the legal battle reached the Supreme Court, critics argued that such federal intrusion into state commerce and individual choice exemplifies the need for a secession mechanism to protect state sovereignty. Unilateral secession provides a pathway for states to escape federal coercion and preserve the autonomy promised by federalism.

Historical Context and Modern Implications

The Civil War’s aftermath entrenched the notion that secession is treasonous, yet this narrative overlooks the Confederacy’s motivations. Southern states seceded not merely to preserve slavery but to resist what they perceived as federal encroachments on their constitutional rights. The Union’s victory, while ending slavery, inadvertently consolidated federal supremacy at the expense of state sovereignty. Subsequent Supreme Court decisions, such as Plessy v. In a modern context, secession could address contemporary grievances absent effective legislative or judicial remedies. For example, states refusing to enforce federal immigration policies or gun control measures could benefit from an unimpeded secession process. This does not imply fracturing the nation gratuitously but underscores the importance of peaceful dissent when federal mandates become unconscionable. By recognizing this right, the Union transforms into a voluntary association, fostering both unity and respect for regional diversity.

Conclusion: A Right to Preserve Liberty

The right to secede is fundamentally about preserving liberty through checks and balances. It is a constitutional safety valve that empowers states to protect their citizens from federal overreach, ensuring the longevity of democratic governance. While the specter of division looms large, history demonstrates that a union sustained by coercion rather than consent is antithetical to the ideals of 1776. By embracing the principles of self-determination and state sovereignty, the United States can honor its founding ethos while adapting to modern challenges. Unilateral secession, far from being rebellious, is a testament to the enduring truth that government’s legitimacy resides in the will of the governed—a truth enshrined in both the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.

Introduction

The right of states to secede is not a relic of antebellum politics or an endorsement of the Confederacy's cause. It is a principle rooted in the deepest foundations of American constitutionalism: popular sovereignty, enumerated powers, the Tenth Amendment, and the revolutionary heritage of 1776. A Union that can only be maintained by force is not a union of consent but a captive arrangement. The Framers understood that legitimate government rests on the ongoing consent of the governed. It is a remedy of last resort, appropriate only when the constitutional compact has been irreparably broken and the federal government has become fundamentally destructive of the ends for which it was instituted. But the right must exist. Without it, the states are not sovereign partners in a federal republic but subjects of an indivisible national government—and that was never the American design.

The United States was founded on the principle that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. The claim that secession is unconstitutional rests on a misreading of history and a willful ignorance of the principles upon which the Union was formed. The Declaration of Independence (1776) explicitly states that governments are instituted to secure the rights of the people, and that when a government becomes destructive of those ends, "it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it, and to institute new Government." If the American colonies had the right to secede from Britain, then the states—having entered the Union voluntarily—must retain the same right to withdraw.

The Articles of Confederation (1781), the first constitution of the United States, explicitly declared that the Union was "perpetual"—yet it also affirmed that each state retained its "sovereignty, freedom, and independence." The Constitution of 1787 was sold to the states as a compact among sovereign entities, not as an irrevocable surrender of their independence. The Tenth Amendment further reinforces this by stating that "the powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." If the federal government exceeds its enumerated powers, the states have not only the right but the duty to resist—up to and including withdrawal.

The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798), authored by James Madison and Thomas Jefferson, asserted that states had the authority to nullify unconstitutional federal laws. If nullification is justified, then secession—the ultimate act of nullification—must also be justified when the federal government becomes systematically oppressive. Even New England states seriously considered secession during the War of 1812 and the Hartford Convention (1814-1815), proving that the principle was widely accepted in early America.

The Civil War (1861-1865) is often cited as "settling" the question of secession, but this is a legal fiction. The Union’s military victory did not erase the moral and constitutional right of secession; it merely established that the federal government would use force to prevent it. If might makes right, then the British Empire was justified in crushing the American Revolution—a proposition no patriot would accept.

II. Self-Determination: The Fundamental Right of Free Peoples

The principle of self-determination is a cornerstone of just governance. If individuals have the right to govern themselves, then political communities—such as states—must also have that right. The United Nations Charter (1945) recognizes self-determination as a fundamental human right, yet the U.S. federal government denies it to its own states while lecturing other nations on democracy.

Today, California and New York impose radical social policies on their citizens, while Texas and Florida resist federal overreach on issues like gun rights, immigration, and education. The federal government has long abandoned the limited role envisioned by the Founders. Through unconstitutional expansions of power—such as the New Deal, the Civil Rights Act (as applied to private business), Obamacare, and the COVID-19 mandates—Washington has transformed itself into an omnipotent leviathan, dictating to states on matters never delegated to it.

When peaceful resistance (nullification, lawsuits, electoral politics) fails, secession becomes the only remaining tool for states to preserve their liberty. The Texas Nationalist Movement, CalExit, and other modern secessionist groups are not extremists—they are the heirs of the American Revolution, asserting the same rights that the Founders did against King George III.

IV. The Moral Case: Secession as an Act of Resistance to Tyranny

If the federal government can ignore the Constitution, spy on citizens, inflate the currency, wage endless wars, and silence dissent, then the states have not only a right but a duty to dissolve their political bonds. Tyranny, whether by a king or a federal bureaucracy, is still tyranny.

The American Revolution was an act of secession. The Confederacy’s secession was wrong on slavery, but right on the principle of state sovereignty. VI. Conclusion: Secession is the Ultimate Check on Tyranny

The right of secession is not about division, but about freedom. It is the final safeguard against an out-of-control federal government. If the states cannot leave, then the Union is not a compact, but a prison.

The Founders understood that governments must be kept in check. When all other checks fail—when the Supreme Court, Congress, and the presidency become instruments of oppression—secession is the people’s last resort. To deny this right is to deny the very principles of 1776.

The time has come to reclaim the right of secession—not as an act of war, but as an act of peaceful, democratic self-determination. The federal government fears secession because it fears losing control. But if the Union is truly based on consent, then let the people decide. Let the states go free.

The Unalienable Right of Secession: Constitutional Foundations, Self-Determination, and the Safeguard Against Federal Tyranny

Introduction

The question of whether a state may lawfully and unilaterally withdraw from the United States strikes at the very heart of the American political experiment. It is a question that has simmered since the founding, erupted in civil war, and remains alive in contemporary debates over federal overreach. This essay contends that individual states retain the inherent right to secede from the Union—a right rooted in the constitutional compact, enshrined in the principle of self‑determination, and indispensable as a check against federal tyranny. While the Union is a great and noble enterprise, its legitimacy derives solely from the consent of the governed; when that consent is withdrawn, no force of arms or judicial decree can rightfully compel a people to remain.

I. Constitutional Principles: The Union as a Compact of Sovereign States

The United States was not created by a monolithic national government delegating power downward, but by sovereign states voluntarily delegating limited authority to a common agent. This compact theory is embedded in the nation’s founding documents and the structure of the Constitution itself.

  • The Declaration of Independence proclaimed the thirteen colonies to be “free and independent states” with “full power to levy war, conclude peace, contract alliances, establish commerce, and to do all other acts and things which independent states may of right do.” The states thus entered the world as separate sovereignties.

  • The Articles of Confederation (1781) expressly declared that “each state retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence.” The Union under the Articles was a league of sovereigns, not a consolidated nation.

  • The Constitution of 1787 was ratified not by a national plebiscite but by conventions of the people in each state. Each state, acting in its sovereign capacity, decided whether to join the new, “more perfect Union.” The ratification process underscores that the federal government is a creature of the states, not the reverse.

  • The Tenth Amendment crystallizes this relationship: “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” Nowhere does the Constitution delegate to the federal government the power to prevent a state from leaving, nor does it prohibit secession. By the plain language of the Tenth Amendment, the right to secede is reserved to the states or the people.

  • Constitutional Silence is equally telling. Had the framers intended to create a perpetual union, they could have included an express prohibition against secession—as they did, for example, against states entering into treaties (Article I, Section 10). Their failure to do so indicates that secession was not foreclosed; indeed, many at the ratifying conventions understood that the states retained the right to withdraw if the compact were violated.

The constitutional design, therefore, rests on the principle that the states are the primary sovereigns. The federal government exercises only those powers that have been loaned to it; the remainder—including the ultimate authority to dissolve the political bonds—remain with the states.

II. Self‑Determination: The Right of a People to Choose Their Government

The American Revolution was fought under the banner of self‑determination. The Declaration of Independence states unequivocally that governments derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed,” and that “whenever any form of government becomes destructive of these ends, it is the right of the people to alter or to abolish it, and to institute new government.” This is not a right limited to the revolutionary generation; it is an enduring principle of American political philosophy.

  • Popular Sovereignty means that the people are the ultimate source of political authority. If the citizens of a state, through a democratic process (such as a referendum or convention), decide that their interests and liberties are no longer served by remaining in the Union, they have a natural right to form a new political association. To deny that right is to deny the very foundation of the American republic.

  • International Precedent further underscores the legitimacy of self‑determination. The United States has repeatedly championed the right of peoples around the world to choose their own destiny—from the revolutions of 1848 to the decolonization movements of the 20th century. Consistency demands that the same principle be honored at home.

  • Secession as the Ultimate Check on government overreach is a logical extension of the social contract theory articulated by John Locke and echoed in the Declaration. When a government persistently violates the terms of the compact, the people may rightfully resume their original sovereignty. Secession is precisely such an act of resumption.

In a nation built on the idea that governments exist by consent, the ability to withdraw consent must be preserved. To argue otherwise is to embrace the very absolutism the American Revolution rejected.

III. Resistance to Federal Overreach: Secession as a Necessary Safeguard

The growth of the federal government since the founding has been staggering. From the New Deal to the Great Society to the modern administrative state, Washington has assumed powers never enumerated in the Constitution, encroaching on areas traditionally reserved to the states. This centralization threatens individual liberty and the balance of federalism.

  • The States as Creators and Guardians of the federal system intended the threat of secession to be a final bulwark against tyranny. James Madison, in The Federalist No. 46, assured the states that “the people . . . could, by the election of more faithful representatives, annul the acts of the usurpers.” But when the federal government itself controls the mechanisms of election and representation, that safeguard may prove inadequate. In such circumstances, the right to exit the compact becomes indispensable.

  • Historical Assertions of the Right demonstrate that states have long viewed secession as a legitimate response to federal overreach.

    • The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (1798–99), authored by Jefferson and Madison, asserted that states have the authority to judge unconstitutional federal acts and to “interpose” to protect their citizens. The resolutions stopped short of advocating secession, but they laid the groundwork for the principle that the states, as parties to the compact, may reclaim delegated powers if the compact is broken.
    • The Hartford Convention (1814–15) saw New England states contemplate secession in response to the oppressive policies of the Madison administration during the War of 1812. Though secession was not enacted, the convention reaffirmed the compact theory and the right of a state to withdraw.
    • The secession of eleven Southern states in 1860–61, whatever one thinks of their motives, was predicated on the belief that the federal government had violated the constitutional compact. While slavery was an abhorrent institution, the underlying constitutional argument—that a state may leave the Union—was shared by many who opposed slavery, including abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, who famously declared, “No Union with slaveholders.”

  • A Deterrent to Tyranny—Even if rarely exercised, the mere possibility of secession disciplines the federal government, reminding it that its powers are limited and that the states are not mere administrative subdivisions. Without such a deterrent, the federal government faces no effective limit to its expansion, leading to the kind of unchecked central authority the framers feared.

The right to secede is thus not a recipe for chaos, but a safety valve that preserves the voluntary nature of the Union and ensures that the federal government remains accountable to the sovereign states that created it.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

Opponents of secession typically raise three objections: that the Civil War settled the issue, that the Supreme Court has ruled secession unconstitutional, and that recognizing a right to secede would lead to anarchy. Each of these arguments fails upon closer examination.

  • The Civil War was a bloody conflict that ended with the defeat of the Confederacy. However, might does not make right. The outcome of a war cannot alter constitutional principle; otherwise, every act of aggression would be self‑justifying. That the Union prevailed militarily does not prove that secession was illegal or immoral—only that it was unsuccessful.

  • Texas v. White (1869) is the Supreme Court case most often cited against secession. Chief Justice Salmon Chase wrote that the Union was “indissoluble” and that secession was “absolutely null.” Yet Chase’s reasoning relied heavily on the Preamble’s reference to “a more perfect Union”—a phrase that is aspirational and not a grant of power. The Court also invoked the Articles of Confederation’s description of a “perpetual Union,” but that language was omitted from the Constitution precisely because the framers rejected the idea of a perpetual league. Moreover, Texas v. White was decided in the shadow of the Civil War and Reconstruction; it is more a political pronouncement than a sound constitutional interpretation. Even after that decision, the Court has never squarely addressed the compact theory that undergirds the right of secession.

  • Fear of Anarchy is understandable but overstated. Secession would not be undertaken lightly; it is a momentous decision that would require overwhelming popular support. History shows that most states value the benefits of union and would not secede without profound grievances. Moreover, a constitutional right to secede does not mean the process would be lawless; it could be regulated by the seceding state’s own laws and by negotiated terms of departure, as occurs in peaceful dissolutions like the Czech–Slovak split. The alternative—forcing a people to remain under a government they reject—is itself a recipe for violence and instability, as the Civil War tragically demonstrated.

Conclusion

The right of a state to secede from the United States is not a radical or novel proposition; it is woven into the fabric of the nation’s founding principles. The Constitution, properly understood, is a compact among sovereign states that retain ultimate authority. The Declaration of Independence enshrines the right of a people to alter or abolish their government. And the inexorable growth of federal power makes the ability to exit the Union an essential safeguard of liberty.

To deny this right is to assert that the federal government holds a monopoly on force, that the consent of the governed is revocable only by revolution, and that the states are mere provinces of an indivisible empire. Such a view is antithetical to the American experiment. A true union is one that is voluntary, sustained by mutual benefit and shared values—not coerced by the sword. By affirming the right of secession, we honor the vision of the founders, protect the principle of self‑determination, and ensure that the federal government remains, as it was intended to be, a servant of the people and the states.

The Right of States to Secede: A Constitutional Defense of Self-Determination and Federalism

The question of whether individual states have the right to unilaterally secede from the United States is one of the most contentious issues in American history. While the Civil War settled the matter in blood, the legal and philosophical foundations of secession remain rooted in the principles of federalism, state sovereignty, and the inherent right to self-determination. The Constitution, far from forbidding secession, was designed to protect the rights of states as independent political entities. By examining the constitutional text, historical precedents, and the moral imperative of self-governance, it becomes clear that states have every right to peacefully withdraw if their interests or principles are no longer aligned with those of the central government.

The Constitutional Compact: A Union of Sovereign States

The U.S. Constitution is not a document of absolute federal supremacy but a compact between sovereign states. The phrase "We the People of the United States" (emphasis added) suggests that the authority of the federal government derives from the states, not the other way around. This was the understanding of the Founders, many of whom explicitly supported the right of states to secede if the Union became oppressive.

Alexander Hamilton, in Federalist No. 28, argued that if the federal government became tyrannical, Americans would have the right to "take up arms" and, in modern terms, dissolve their political ties. Thomas Jefferson, in his Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, declared that when the federal government exceeded its constitutional authority, states had the right—not just the duty—to nullify unconstitutional laws or withdraw from the Union. James Madison, the "Father of the Constitution," also acknowledged in Federalist No. 46 that states could resist federal overreach through "every legal means" and even resort to separation if necessary.

The Supremacy Clause (Article VI, Clause 2) states that federal law is supreme only when acting within its enumerated powers. If the federal government exceeds those powers—whether through unconstitutional mandates, economic coercion, or cultural imperialism—a state retains the right to declare such actions null and void and, if necessary, leave the Union. The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people all powers not delegated to the federal government, reinforcing the idea that the Union is voluntary.

Historical Precedent: Secession Before the Civil War

Before the Civil War, secession was not an unthinkable concept but a recognized tool of political resistance. The New England states, facing federal policies they opposed (such as the War of 1812 and later the Tariff of Abominations), openly discussed secession. The Hartford Convention of 1814-1815, though ultimately failing to secure secession, demonstrated that Northern states were willing to consider separation when federal policies harmed their interests.

The Southern states, in their secession declarations, explicitly cited violations of the constitutional compact. South Carolina’s Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession (1860) stated that the federal government had overstepped its authority by attempting to abolish slavery, violating the property rights of Southern states. While the Civil War resulted in the military suppression of secession, it did not legally settle the issue—since the South was forcibly reintegrated, no constitutional amendment or Supreme Court ruling explicitly forbade future secessions.

The modern insistence that the Union is "permanent" and secession is "illegal" is ahistorical. The federal government’s claim of perpetual union stems from the Texas v. White (1869) decision, where the Supreme Court (under Reconstruction-era pressures) ruled that secession was unlawful. However, this was a politically motivated ruling aimed at preventing further Southern resistance, not a grounded interpretation of constitutional law. As legal scholar Jeffrey Hummel argues in Emancipating Slaves, Enslaving Free Men, the Court had no proper authority to invalidate a sovereign act of secession—especially since the Confederacy was not a party to the case and had already been destroyed by war.

If the Union were truly indissoluble, the Constitution would have included an explicit prohibition on secession, just as the Articles of Confederation (which the Constitution replaced) had no such ban. The absence of such a provision in the Constitution underscores the Founders’ belief that the Union was a voluntary association.

The modern federal government has vastly exceeded its constitutional limits, justifying state resistance—and potentially secession—as a last resort. Through unconstitutional spending (e.g., Medicare, welfare programs not authorized by Article I, Section 8), regulatory overreach (e.g., the EPA, FDA, and DOJ dictating state policies), and judicial activism (e.g., Roe v. Wade, Obergefell v. Hodges), the federal government has become a Leviathan unaccountable to the states.

The principle of remedial secession—where states may peacefully withdraw if the Union becomes oppressive—was recognized by the international community in the case of Kosovo’s 2008 independence from Serbia. If a state can intervene militarily to protect human rights, why can’t a state withdraw to protect its own sovereignty?

Many contemporary issues justify renewed consideration of secession:

  • Second Amendment Nullification: States like California and New York have effectively banned certain firearms, ignoring the Constitution’s prohibition on state interference with "the right to keep and bear arms" (via the 14th Amendment).
  • Anti-Immigration Federalism: Federal failure to secure the border has forced states like Texas to take direct action, raising questions about whether such neglect justifies severing ties.
  • Cultural and Religious Discrimination: States facing federal mandates on gender ideology, healthcare, and education (e.g., transgender mandates on children) may reasonably conclude that continued union is untenable.
  • Economic Coercion: The federal government’s control over funding (e.g., highway dollars, Medicaid expansion) allows it to dictate state policies, effectively imposing a de facto unitary system.

If the federal government will not reform, states must have the constitutional right to peacefully exit the Union rather than submit to tyranny.

Conclusion: The Moral and Constitutional Right to Self-Determination

The right of states to secede is not a relic of a bygone era but a living principle of self-determination essential to liberty. The Constitution, as originally understood, was a compact among sovereign states—not an all-powerful central government. Federal overreach, economic exploitation, and cultural subjugation have made the modern Union oppressive in ways the Founders warned against.

Those who oppose secession often invoke the specter of chaos or racial injustice, forgetting that the Civil War’s horrors resulted from federal coercion, not Southern secession. A peaceful, gradual, and democratic process of state withdrawal is not an act of rebellion but a reassertion of the principles of federalism and consent of the governed.

If the United States is truly a "government of the people, by the people, for the people," then the people of the states must retain the ultimate right to determine their political future. The alternative—eternal federal domination—is the antithesis of liberty. The right to secede is not a fringe idea but a fundamental check against tyranny, ensuring that the Union remains a voluntary association rather than a prison of the states.

The Right of States to Secede: A Constitutional and Moral Imperative

Introduction

The original Constitution was ratified by the states, not by the federal government alone. The Tenth Amendment explicitly reserves all powers not delegated to the federal government to the states or the people, reinforcing that the Union is a compact among sovereign entities, not a unitary state.

If states entered the Union by their own consent, they retain the right to withdraw by the same consent—a principle recognized in international law and confirmed by the Declaration of Independence.

B. The Right to Revolution and Self-Government

The Declaration of Independence established that governments exist only by the consent of the governed. When a government violates this compact—through tyranny, oppression, or unconstitutional expansion of power—the people have not only the right but the duty to resist. The Founders understood this principle well; they revolted against British rule precisely because it violated their natural and constitutional rights.

Today, the federal government has repeatedly overstepped its constitutional bounds:

  • Unfunded mandates forcing states to comply with federal laws they did not consent to (e.g., Obamacare’s individual mandate).

  • Judicial and executive usurpation of state sovereignty, as seen in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), where the Supreme Court expanded federal power beyond constitutional limits.

The right to self-determination is a cornerstone of modern democracy. Nations and peoples have the right to govern themselves without coercion.
